title: TimeOmni-VL: Unified Models for Time Series Understanding and Generation
one_liner: A single model can understand what's happening in time series data AND accurately generate future values by converting both to images, then solving both tasks together.
lead: When you study a time series like stock prices or temperature, two kinds of work clash: one model learns to describe what's happening (prices rising means an opportunity), and another tries to predict the next number exactly right. TimeOmni-VL merges these by turning time series into pictures, so a single model solves both jobs at once.

problem.h2: Time series are split between two dead ends
paras: Today's models split into two types. One kind learns to read time series numbers and answer questions: 'Is the trend up or down? Is this normal or an anomaly?' That model is okay at the concepts but terrible at writing out the actual next numbers—it guesses 5.2 when it should be 5.17. The other kind is the opposite: it obsesses over predicting the exact next number with high precision, but it ignores whether that number makes sense in context.

A beginner would try one model for understanding and swap to another for generation. But then you train twice, and they contradict each other: the understanding model learned to ignore small wiggles because they don't matter conceptually, while the generation model learned to lock onto those exact wiggles.

callout.html: Models built for understanding ignore numerical precision; models built for precision ignore the big picture.

steps.text: Turn the numbers into pixel heights and shades; this works because vision models are built to spot shapes and trends in pictures, and height/color is how images naturally encode magnitude and rate of change.
Teach the model to read the image and name patterns: 'Is this trending up? Is this an anomaly?'
Teach it to predict the next numbers in the image, guided by what it learned about the pattern.

steps.b: Use understanding as a control signal
steps.text: When generating, force the model to first state what it thinks is happening, then commit to numbers that match that story.
One forward pass gives you a semantic label and a high-precision forecast.

paras: TimeOmni-VL changes how a model sees time series data: instead of treating numbers as opaque lists, it converts them into images. An image has spatial structure (left-to-right is time; height is magnitude), so visual reasoning models built for photos can transfer their understanding to time series.

hidden.name: Semantic alignment score
paras: The paper measures how much a generated forecast matches the semantic story the model learned. If the model says 'this is a rising trend,' but generates numbers that fall, the alignment is low. Alignment is the degree to which understanding and generation agree on the big picture.

The paper estimates alignment by having the model first state what it understands (using a chain-of-thought, which is an explicit step-by-step reasoning trace), then checking whether the generated numbers are consistent with that reasoning. High alignment means the model's story and its numbers tell the same tale.

heat.caption: Darker means higher semantic alignment (understanding and generation agree).

reads.html: Semantic alignment measures whether the model's explanation (what it thinks is happening) matches its prediction (what it thinks comes next).
The paper quantifies alignment by running both understanding and generation, then checking cross-consistency: does the chain-of-thought explanation predict the numerical output?

paras: Converting time series to images taps into years of multimodal training. Models trained on vision datasets already understand structure: high pixels mean big values, color transitions mean trends, clusters mean patterns. When you show a time series as an image, the model recognizes these structures without starting from scratch.

Teaching understanding first anchors the model's reasoning. When you force the model to first state 'I see a rising trend' or 'This is a seasonal cycle,' you create a semantic contract it must honor later. If it then predicts falling numbers, the contract is broken, and the training loss says so. This constraint—forcing coherence between explanation and prediction—prevents the two tasks from drifting apart.

The model never has to choose between understanding and precision. Understanding tasks (Is this an anomaly?) teach high-level pattern recognition. Generation tasks (What is the next number?) teach fine detail. Because both run in the same forward pass and share representations, the model learns to do both at once: high-level patterns guide the fine-grained prediction toward realism.

stages.s: Reasoning step: state what you see
Generate next numbers, constrained by reasoning

math.words: The total loss is a weighted sum of understanding loss and generation loss, plus a penalty for semantic misalignment. The penalty term is high when the model's stated understanding contradicts its numerical forecast.
math.equation: L_total = L_understand + lambda_gen * L_generate + lambda_align * mismatch(reasoning, forecast)
symbols: loss when the model predicts semantic labels; measures how often it correctly identifies trends, anomalies
loss when the model predicts the next number; measures how far off its forecast is from the true value
weight controlling how much generation matters relative to understanding
weight controlling how much we penalize contradiction between reasoning and numbers
a score that grows large if the semantic label contradicts the numerical output (e.g., reasoning says rising but forecast says falling)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the true next value is 5.2, the model understands correctly (label is right), and forecasts 5.1.
Now suppose the model understands correctly but forecasts 4.5, contradicting its stated trend.
The model learns to avoid contradiction because it raises the loss steeply.

math.note: The alignment penalty acts as a referee: it forces understanding and generation to tell the same story.

charts.title: Separate models
charts.note: Training two models separately: understanding is okay, generation lacks precision, and they contradict.

charts.title: TimeOmni-VL unified
charts.note: One model trained end-to-end: understanding improves slightly because the image representation is richer, generation is much more precise because semantic guidance anchors it toward realistic numbers that match the stated pattern, and they align because the loss function penalizes contradiction.

items.b: Image conversion loses information if not designed carefully.
items.html: If pixel shades are coarse, two very different time series could render to identical images, making them indistinguishable at generation time. The solution: design the color scale so that each distinct pixel shade maps to a small, unique range of numbers. This way, when the model sees a particular shade, it can accurately invert it back to the right number range.
If the model's semantic reasoning is wrong, the generation penalty drags the forecast further from correct numbers rather than closer. A false understanding becomes a false anchor.

items.b: Scaling breaks for very long series.
items.html: Long time series convert to very wide images. Vision models are built for photos, not ultra-wide inputs. Some patterns might disappear at the resolution limit.

The paper's bidirectional mapping (TS-to-image and image-to-TS) is carefully calibrated to preserve numerical fidelity: pixel heights directly encode magnitude, color encodes derivative (how fast it's changing), and the conversion is invertible so nothing is lost. Semantic reasoning is trained first on ground-truth labels, so it learns true patterns before it constrains generation.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple dataset: stock prices over 100 days. Hand-label five understanding tasks for each series: Is this trending up, down, or flat? Is there an anomaly in the last 10 days? Does it have a seasonal cycle? Then split the series: train on days 1–80, predict days 81–90, and evaluate days 91–100.
Train a TimeOmni-VL model: convert series to images, run understanding tasks, generate the missing days, measure both accuracy on the labels and numerical distance to ground truth.

Compare: a model trained only on generation (ignoring understanding) will forecast lower precision and contradict any labels you ask for. TimeOmni-VL should beat it on precision and maintain semantic consistency.
demo.metric_eq: coherence = min(understanding_accuracy, generation_precision) / max(understanding_accuracy, generation_precision); higher means the two tasks support each other
demo.closing: The demo must show that semantic guidance raises precision: understanding steers generation toward realistic numbers that make sense in context.
